Coding Standards

To keep the project maintainable, let's follow a few rules:

One class per file.
Engine.js coordinates systems only—it shouldn't contain detailed game logic.
All game data (quests, NPCs, buildings, problems) lives in separate data files.
UI panels never draw themselves directly from game logic; a UIManager controls visibility and layout.
New features should plug into existing systems rather than adding more conditionals to the engine.
I also suggest we start using Git properly

A simple commit history will make it much easier to experiment:

main
│
├── v0.1 Initial engine
├── v0.2 UI refactor
├── v0.3 Sprite rendering
├── v0.4 Living city
├── v0.5 Startup gameplay
└── v1.0 First playable release

That way, if a change breaks something, you can always roll back to the last working version.

Next milestone

The very next thing I'd build is the UI refactor:

UIManager.js
NotificationManager.js
A redesigned HUD
A clean dialogue window
Smooth open/close animations
A proper top status bar
No more flickering or overlapping panels

Once that's in place, every new feature will feel much more polished and the codebase will be much easier to grow.

ok

I think this is exactly the right time to reset and build the game properly.

🚀 Startup World v0.2

Instead of patching individual files, we'll build a small game engine with clear systems.

Core Principles
🎮 Gameplay first
🧩 Modular code
🎨 Easy to reskin with sprites
📱 GitHub Pages compatible
⚡ Vanilla JavaScript only
📦 No frameworks
🔧 Easy to expand
Architecture
StartupWorld
│
├── Engine
│
├── Renderer
│
├── Camera
│
├── Input
│
├── World
│
├── EntityManager
│
├── UIManager
│
├── QuestManager
│
├── DialogueManager
│
├── CompanyManager
│
├── SaveManager
│
└── AudioManager

Notice that Engine never contains game logic.

Instead it becomes something like:

update(dt) {
    this.input.update(dt);

    this.world.update(dt);

    this.entities.update(dt);

    this.company.update(dt);

    this.ui.update(dt);

    this.camera.update(dt);
}

render() {
    this.renderer.begin();

    this.world.draw();

    this.entities.draw();

    this.ui.draw();

    this.renderer.end();
}

That's the direction we want.

The World

Instead of lots of arrays inside World.js, we'll create map layers.

NPC System

Instead of plain objects:

{

}

    draw(){}

    interact(){}

}

Every NPC behaves the same way.

One change I'd make

Rather than continuing to hand-edit every file in chat, I'd suggest we build the project one complete subsystem at a time:

Engine Refactor
UI System
Rendering & Sprites
World System
Gameplay Systems

Each subsystem will be fully working before we move to the next. That keeps the project stable, avoids regressions like the UI flickering you've seen, and makes it much easier to add ambitious features later.

I think that's the fastest route to turning this into a polished, explorable startup world rather than an ever-growing prototype.
